explanation:
The C++ Standard Library provides overloaded comparison operators (`==`, `!=`, `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=`) for `std::pair`. These comparisons require that the constituent types T1 and T2 also support the corresponding comparison operators.

Equality (`==`):
Two pairs, p1 and p2, are equal if and only if `p1.first == p2.first` AND `p1.second == p2.second`. This requires T1 and T2 to be equality comparable.

Ordering (`<`):
Ordering is defined lexicographically. `p1 < p2` is true if:
1. `p1.first < p2.first` (T1 determines the order), OR
2. `p1.first == p2.first` AND `p1.second < p2.second` (T2 determines the order only if T1 components are equal).

Technical Details:
This lexicographical ordering is essential when `std::pair` is used as a key in ordered associative containers (like `std::map`, `std::set`), as these containers rely on a strict weak ordering. If T1 and T2 provide O(C1) and O(C2) comparison complexity, the pair comparison complexity is typically O(C1 + C2) in the worst case (when T1 components are equal) or O(C1) on average.
practical_example: Using `std::pair<int, int>` to represent 2D coordinates in a `std::set`. The lexicographical comparison automatically orders the coordinates, allowing efficient lookup based first on the X-coordinate, and then on the Y-coordinate if X-coordinates match.
book: The C++ Standard Library: A Tutorial and Reference by Nicolai M. Josuttis
